items.why: Attribution by others is plausible context, not proof; check timeline and whether difficulties preceded the event.

items.question: How do I tell deciding before checking the facts, as a quick-to-act sign, from carelessness that follows low mood?

key_points.text: Acting before checking, such as ordering a large item and measuring afterwards, reads as an impulsive sequence or executive slip rather than mere carelessness.
key_points.condition: stronger if repeated across purchases or domains

key_points.text: Acting before the other person has answered (pulling signs down, snapping in public) is read by many as impulsive action preceding social processing.
key_points.condition: weak if a single incident

key_points.text: Low mood since winter or a break-up offers a better explanation for careless spending, irritability and loss of regard for consequences, so a flat mood should be set against the impulsivity reading.
key_points.condition: when the low mood predates or accompanies the behaviour

key_points.text: Low mood tends to show as avoidance, inertia and reduced drive rather than distractibility or quick action, so friction that is emotional rather than cognitive points to mood.
key_points.condition: when execution is smooth once the person gets going

key_points.text: To tell the two apart ask whether the pattern appears across domains and over time, whether it was present before the mood change, and whether the low mood is chronic or episodic.
key_points.condition: needs history and a baseline; a single text cannot settle it

key_points.text: A strong external reward such as a staff discount, or free returns, lowers the threshold for impulse buying in anyone.
key_points.condition: when the purchase is tied to a discount or reversible

key_points.text: A self-aware remark such as 'obviously' marks the error as a slip, not a constant state, and a junior may over-read a single impulsive moment or conversely over-diagnose depression and miss co-occurring ADHD.

items.why: Look for a lifelong pattern of acting first versus a recent change; mood context; consequences and awareness.

items.question: In a very organised, list-based message, how much should one small unresolved practical item count?

key_points.text: One acknowledged, low-stakes pending item (laundry) in an otherwise tight plan is a minor omission and not a pattern of neglect; it should count for very little.
key_points.condition: when the item is single, acknowledged and low-stakes

key_points.text: A genuinely unresolved decision, like what fits the new garage, reflects a real spatial constraint and deliberation rather than avoidance, and is ordinary.
key_points.condition: when the writer has already acted on it (asked someone) or needs more information

key_points.text: Maintained external systems and early planning (labelled and numbered boxes, a master sheet, early bookings) point away and outweigh a small loose end.
key_points.condition: though if the organisation is only situational high-stakes effort the baseline is unknown

key_points.text: An uncertain count (eleven or twelve photos) is ordinary estimation or casual memory and not a deficit.
A few clinicians read the loose ends (laundry, photo count) as faint hints of task-initiation or tracking difficulty, but all call it minor.
key_points.condition: weak, and only if the same pattern recurs

key_points.text: A repeated, costly backlog (six unsent invoices, 'I keep saying I'll do them') counts for more than a single small item, though long working days confound it.
key_points.condition: when intention repeatedly fails to turn into action over weeks

key_points.text: A baseline is needed to weigh any loose end: other texts from an ordinary week, whether the writer is usually this organised, and what happened with earlier tasks.
Follow up whether the item is a one-off or part of a pattern of delayed tasks and whether the promised action happened.

anchor.passage: Laundry is the one thing I haven't sorted.

items.why: A single loose end in an otherwise tidy plan is ordinary; list style signals planning; do not over-read it.

items.question: How can I separate working-memory lapses from the ordinary forgetfulness of a poor-sleep week when all I have is a short written sample?

key_points.text: Poor sleep, fatigue, stress, anxiety or low mood impair working memory in almost anyone, so lapses such as walking into a room and forgetting why are very common and often better explained by state than by trait.
key_points.condition: when the writer reports sleep debt, new surroundings or acute stress

key_points.text: State-versus-trait is separated by whether lapses occur when the person is rested, calm or on easy or interesting tasks, and across settings; if only when tired or stressed it is likely situational.
key_points.condition: only if the lapses persist when rested and across settings

key_points.text: A short text cannot decide this; one needs a sample from a calm well-rested day, repeated accounts, baseline history including childhood, and possibly a structured questionnaire.
Specific lapses of losing the intention despite a list, or starting and dropping a task, are more suggestive of working-memory slips but are still sleep-sensitive and a single instance proves little.
key_points.condition: only if they recur outside sleep debt or stress

key_points.text: Low frequency, such as two occurrences in a short post or one episode, does not show a pervasive pattern, so do not over-read it.
key_points.condition: when the lapse is isolated or brief

key_points.text: Errors with a named external cause (a local file nobody mentioned, a faulty handover) are systems failures rather than memory failures, so first ask whether the error was caused by something outside the writer.
key_points.condition: when the writer names a plausible external cause

key_points.text: Self-monitoring, planning and coherent structure in the text count against a working-memory problem; a less experienced clinician may over-pathologise a tired person's bad week.

items.labeller_note: No note offers a decisive discriminating sign from text alone; they mainly say get a baseline and more samples.
items.why: Look for lapses on well-rested stretches, lifelong history, compensations, and whether the writer links lapses to sleep.

items.question: How should I read bulleted, telegraphic or fragmentary writing: sign of disorganisation, or just the format the writer chose?

key_points.text: A terse, lower-case or greeting-free style is often just how a writer addresses family or friends and is not by itself evidence of disorganisation.
key_points.condition: when the content is otherwise ordered

key_points.text: Judge the logic and coherence rather than the surface form: a stream of technical details can be a tight chain of cause and effect, and a sequenced account is the opposite of the scattered narrative expected in disorganisation.
key_points.condition: when events follow in order and the text returns to its point

key_points.text: To decide whether the fragmentary style is the writer's norm, compare with another text from an ordinary or calm day.

items.labeller_note: No note deals directly with bulleted or telegraphic format; only a lower-case email style and coherence of structure are covered.
items.why: Format reflects medium and haste; judge coherence and content, not brevity; compare with the same writer's other registers.

items.question: What does a writer correcting themselves mid-sentence or changing a plan in the last line tell me, if anything?

key_points.text: Noticing and correcting a digression or slip in the text ('Anyway', 'sorry', 'caught myself', 'I told myself') shows intact self-monitoring and awareness, which argues against severe executive dysfunction.
key_points.condition: when the writer returns to the main point straight away

key_points.text: The drift that needed correcting still happened: a derailed thought cut off mid-sentence, or a self-catch alongside poor impulse control, can reflect attentional drift despite preserved metacognition.
key_points.condition: mild unless the drifts recur

key_points.text: Self-aware irony about an error ('obviously') shows insight but does not remove the planning gap; it can mean the error was a slip and not a constant state.
A last-line change of plan ('tomorrow, or actually tonight') may show a split between intention and execution.
key_points.condition: weak, one reading from a single phrase

key_points.text: Ask whether the digression or self-correction is habitual or a one-off, and do not over-read it as inattention or miss it as a sign of good social cognition.

items.labeller_note: Few notes address mid-sentence correction or last-line plan changes directly; most are about other fragments.
items.why: Self-correction is common and often reflects care; consider frequency and whether it blocks the message.

items.question: A patient shows delayed starting on tasks but recently lost a parent. What do I ask next to decide whether the delay is meaningful?

key_points.text: Ask whether the delayed starting was present before the parent died or began only after the loss; a new onset points to grief or a situational response rather than a lifelong trait.
key_points.condition: if the delay is new since the bereavement or a recent stressor

key_points.text: A pattern that has been consistent across years, back into earlier life, favours a trait rather than a reaction to recent loss.
key_points.condition: only if the delay is documented across long periods before the loss

key_points.text: Ask whether the stalling recurs across settings (work, leisure, other tasks) or is a one-off or confined to the high-stress context.
key_points.condition: cross-setting recurrence raises the case, a single stressful context lowers it

key_points.text: Grief, poor sleep and low mood can themselves cause brain fog and difficulty initiating tasks, so sleep and mood (and anxiety) need to be clarified, for example with a sleep diary.
Check whether the stalled task is emotionally specific (tied to the bereavement) while other tasks are completed normally, which argues against a general initiation problem.
key_points.condition: if other, non-emotional tasks are done competently

key_points.text: Ask what the person felt or thought while not starting; fear of getting it wrong or anxious avoidance can look like an initiation problem.
key_points.condition: if the delay is driven by anxiety or fear of error

key_points.text: Obtain a sample of current work or writing from a calm day, and baseline functioning, to see whether lapses persist when stress and grief are lower.

items.labeller_note: Notes are readings of patient texts, none is a direct how-to for grief plus delayed starting; the questions to ask must be inferred from several notes.
items.why: Ask about onset, pre-bereavement pattern, childhood history, and whether delay is task-specific or global.

items.question: How do I separate a low-mood drop in effort on dull tasks from lifelong difficulty holding attention on them?

key_points.text: Establish onset: whether the attention or effort difficulty is lifelong (school, earlier jobs, childhood reports) or new since the bereavement or low mood.
key_points.condition: lifelong history raises the case; onset after the low mood lowers it

key_points.text: Ask whether the person wants to start but cannot (executive friction, favouring ADHD) or simply does not feel like doing anything (mood, anhedonia, lethargy); also whether the problem is focus or drive.
Check whether the lapses also occur on non-aversive, interesting or low-stakes tasks and across settings; if only on dull or stressful tasks, mood or stress is the better explanation.
key_points.condition: pervasive across tasks and settings raises; confined to aversive tasks lowers

key_points.text: Bereavement and low mood readily explain sitting and doing little and loss of effort on a dull job (grief, anhedonia, fatigue), and tell nothing about a lifelong pattern.
key_points.condition: when grief or low mood is documented alongside the lapse

key_points.text: Drifting to side tasks (comparing apps, reorganising folders) is ordinary procrastination on a dull task, made worse by low mood, anxiety or fatigue, and is not specific to ADHD.
key_points.condition: when mood, anxiety or grief are present

key_points.text: Side-task drift on an aversive task can be a typical ADHD-style avoidance or workaround, so it cannot be dismissed, but it is ambiguous between ADHD and low mood.
Sleep, fatigue, deadline stress and anxiety should be assessed (mood and anxiety ratings, sleep) because acute state factors can produce the same lapses as a trait.
key_points.condition: if lapses occur only under fatigue or stress

key_points.text: Request a writing sample from a calm, rested day or a diary of routine tasks over weeks to separate stable cognitive style from acute state.
Preserved self-monitoring, coping strategies and organised or verifying behaviour (timer, written list, noticing oneself drift) argue against a severe lifelong executive deficit.
Low mood can mask or co-occur with ADHD traits, so avoid diagnosing depression or ADHD alone and ask whether low mood is chronic or episodic.

items.labeller_note: No note directly compares depressive effort loss with lifelong inattention in general terms; points are drawn from readings of grief-related patient texts.
items.why: Onset and course, anhedonia, pervasiveness beyond dull tasks, and what holds attention when mood is better.

items.question: What do less experienced clinicians tend to over-read in a single journal entry about time estimation?

key_points.text: Less experienced clinicians over-read a single planned-versus-actual time overrun (two hours became the evening, an hour became three) as time blindness or ADHD, when it is common under stress, fatigue, workload or a harder-than-expected task.
key_points.condition: when it is a single episode

key_points.text: They ignore context that explains the overrun: poor sleep after a move, deadline stress, high cognitive load, tiredness and anxiety.
External or situational causes given in the text (missing boot, jammed zip, site problems, a colleague's request) account for the delay and should not be read as a trait.
key_points.condition: if the text itself states the cause

key_points.text: They overlook signs of competence, planning and self-monitoring in the same text ('told myself' shows a plan, work completed, organised routine, high achievement elsewhere).

They over-weight distraction or task-switching episodes (a broken link, a phone check) and avoidance of a feared task as ADHD inattention, when the distraction is a symptom of avoidance, anxiety or ordinary human error.
They treat routine reminders or to-do notes ('need to remember to ask Dan') as forgetfulness symptoms.
Anxiety, perfectionism, low mood or burnout are alternative explanations for the overrun and the procrastination around it.
Before reading anything into it, ask whether the person always misestimates time or this was a one-off under pressure, and look at how routine the avoidance pattern is.
Conversely, a clinician may under-read a real estimation or initiation difficulty by blaming tiredness alone, especially if it persists once sleep improves.
key_points.condition: if the time-management problem remains after the sleep issue resolves or recurs

key_points.text: A time-estimation error is a plausible ADHD cue and counts as a weak toward-signal, but one episode carries little weight alone.
key_points.condition: stronger only if it recurs

items.labeller_note: Notes are mostly about one specific diary and come from clinicians of varying experience; they address over-reading directly but with little general guidance beyond the same diary context.
items.why: One bad day or a story with external causes is not a trait; need repeated and cross-setting examples.

items.question: Exam-period writing often shows scattered concentration. How do I decide between worry and distractibility?

key_points.text: Exam or deadline anxiety is a strong alternative: attention frays, narrows, or the person stalls and seeks comfort (coffee, food, side tasks), so scattered concentration in exam week is expected under stress.
key_points.condition: when the text sits in an exam or deadline period

key_points.text: Ask whether this is new or a lifelong pattern: a one-off bad week or first major deadline versus history of similar lapses (school, earlier years, past jobs).
key_points.condition: a lifelong history raises; a first-time stress week lowers

key_points.text: Ask whether the distractibility also appears in low-stakes, interesting or non-academic settings (work, home, relationships) and in weeks without an exam; if only under high-stakes pressure, it favours worry.
key_points.condition: pervasive across settings raises; only under exam pressure lowers

key_points.text: Check sleep, caffeine and fatigue, which mimic ADHD symptoms.
key_points.condition: if short sleep or heavy caffeine accompanies the lapses

key_points.text: Probe the character of the lapse: whether the person wanted to work but lost the thread automatically (working memory or impulsive grab, favouring ADHD) or avoided the task by stalling (anxiety, procrastination); also whether they feel restless or paralysed by worry.
Obtain a writing sample from a calm, no-deadline day for comparison.
Planning, structured work blocks, productive bursts and self-monitoring in the same text argue against a severe attentional problem and point to a competent writer under stress.
A single minor distraction (broken link, bins, toastie) is ordinary human behaviour and a risk for over-reading by junior clinicians.
key_points.condition: when it is an isolated episode

key_points.text: Repeated episodes where the original intent is lost mid-task (forgot why, abandoned the plan) do give some toward-signal for attentional regulation, though stress is a confounder.
key_points.condition: if the pattern recurs and is unintended

items.labeller_note: Strong coverage from notes on one exam-week text; general decision rules for worry versus distractibility are not stated directly outside that case.
items.why: Check timing relative to the stressor, bodily symptoms, avoidance of the feared task versus pulled off any task.

items.question: Late paperwork and invoices are common in busy self-employed people. When does that point to starting difficulty rather than workload?

key_points.text: Long working days, exhaustion, burnout and a recent workload spike readily explain late invoices, since paperwork is the first thing to go for busy self-employed people; check sleep and fatigue too.
key_points.condition: when the backlog coincides with long hours or a busy spell

key_points.text: Establish the timeline: whether the backlog began only with the busy period or existed in quieter years and before the workload rose; a long-standing 'I'll do it Sunday' pattern is a trait, a recent change is load or mood.
key_points.condition: present for years and in quiet periods raises; new since the busy spell lowers

key_points.text: Ask whether other admin (tax, insurance, emails, personal paperwork) is also put off, including on days off or when rested; if only invoices under load, it is a workflow problem, not a starting difficulty.
key_points.condition: cross-domain avoidance raises; only invoicing under load lowers

key_points.text: Repeated intention without follow-through with vague deferral words ('soon', 'usually Sunday', 'after tea'), a long gap between intending and doing, and a real cost such as a five-week-old invoice, points toward a starting difficulty.
key_points.condition: if the gap between intending and doing is long and recurring

key_points.text: Starting a task and stopping at the first small friction point (typing the customer address) is the most specific initiation marker, but fatigue or a distraction could account for it.

Intact planning, competent trade work (accurate quotes for known jobs, completed consumer-unit swap) and a coherent, self-correcting account argue the difficulty is specific to administration under load rather than a global initiation deficit.
Overrunning quotes are better explained by genuine site factors than by time blindness, so they should not be counted as support for starting difficulty.
key_points.condition: when the text gives specific site reasons

key_points.text: Low mood, burnout or ordinary procrastination can look like the same inertia; the experienced reading is to avoid both over-pathologising a tired tradesman and dismissing the deferral wording.
To tell initiation from complexity, look at how the invoice process actually goes and whether earlier systems or apps were tried and failed.

items.labeller_note: All relevant notes read one tradesman's forum post; there is no general guidance on self-employed paperwork, so rules are inferred from that case.
items.why: Compare tasks done on time, availability of free time, and whether the delay predates the workload.

items.question: Where do experienced clinicians disagree when reading irritability or sharp reactions in short texts?

key_points.text: Disagreement over acting before the other person answers (pulling the signs down, snapping in public): some read it as impulsivity and poor error tolerance, a toward-signal for ADHD.
key_points.condition: if it reflects a recurrent lack of pause rather than one incident

key_points.text: Other clinicians read the same sharp reaction as stress, anger, low mood after a break-up, strain or a short night, and decline to read a trait; some say it carries no ADHD signal either way.
key_points.condition: when a stressor or low mood is documented

key_points.text: Irritability described as 'short with everyone' is split between sleep deprivation or chronic noise and stress (most clinicians) and ADHD-related irritability or emotional dysregulation (a minority).
key_points.condition: depends on whether the irritability tracks sleep loss and is absent when rested

key_points.text: Explicit self-monitoring and attribution ('that's the noise, not me', owning the outburst) is read by many as intact insight and regulation, arguing against dysregulation.
Structured, logged, orderly accounts are read as counter-evidence to ADHD by several clinicians, while others warn that orderly structure does not exclude it or that logging is a crisis response.
key_points.condition: depends on whether the organisation is the writer's baseline

key_points.text: Ask about baseline: whether outbursts are new (before the break-up or noise), occur when rested, repeat across contexts, and whether the same reaction recurs ('third time'); a calm-day sample and sleep history are needed.
Junior clinicians tend to over-read outbursts and irritability as impulsivity or emotional dysregulation without checking the sleep, stress or break-up context.
Confusion about a procedure (not sure whether to switch the recorder on) is read as a weak inattention cue by one clinician but as ordinary unfamiliarity or anxiety by most.

items.labeller_note: Notes cover two texts (shop manager outburst, noise and sleep post) and show disagreement indirectly through different readings of the same lines; no clinician names a disagreement explicitly.
items.why: Trait versus situational stress or mood; regret and speed of recovery; need history across settings.

items.question: Beyond what a short written sample shows, what is the minimum I need before treating these features as meaningful?

key_points.text: A single short text is not enough; repeated observations across different days, including a sample written on a calm or low-stress day (or a structured diary), are needed to see whether the pattern is stable.
Evidence that the pattern occurs across settings (work, home, social, school) and causes impairment in at least two life domains, not only in the situation described.
key_points.condition: only if the pattern recurs across settings and causes impairment

key_points.text: A history of onset and duration: early or childhood onset and persistence versus a recent change (new since a stressor, a move, a job, a loss, a busy spell).
key_points.condition: early onset and persistence raises; recent onset after a stressor lowers

key_points.text: Rule out or quantify confounders before reading anything into the features: sleep (ideally a sleep diary), mood, anxiety, grief and situational stress.
key_points.condition: if these explain the features

key_points.text: Collateral information (a partner, friend or colleague who observes the behaviour) and a structured interview, rating scale or executive-function assessment are needed.
One anecdote, even a delayed email or a single vignette, does not suffice for diagnostic inference; features remain ambiguous without longitudinal data.
Context about the writer's usual functioning, responsibilities and personal circumstances is missing and is needed before judging whether the features are characteristic.

items.labeller_note: Notes give the minimum information consistently but as caveats on single texts; no explicit threshold such as number of settings or samples is stated beyond 'at least two domains'.
items.why: Childhood onset, impairment across settings, collateral, current stressors and sleep, substance use.

items.question: How do I distinguish enthusiasm for new hobbies from novelty-seeking, especially in someone with a young child at home?

key_points.text: A new project started straight after seeing a single video, displacing the current project, reads as an impulsive switch of priority that leans toward novelty-seeking.
The same switch is often ordinary enthusiasm, inspiration, boredom or a need for stimulation that any hobbyist shows.
key_points.condition: if it is a one-off burst of excitement rather than a habit

key_points.text: To tell them apart, ask whether the person routinely drops projects for new ones, and whether the new idea replaces the old project or is just a nice-to-have.
key_points.condition: a repeated pattern of abandonment points to a trait; a single episode does not

key_points.text: With a young child at home, sleep loss, fragmented time (work only in naps) and the need for stimulation in the childcare period can produce scattered attention and project-hopping without ADHD.
key_points.condition: if the pattern is absent when rested or before the child, and organised on a full night's sleep

key_points.text: Useful missing information: whether this is new since the baby or lifelong, whether it shows in other domains such as work, and a text from a calm day.
Clinicians warn against over-reading the new-project impulse as impulsivity, though one warns that dismissing it as mere interest could under-read a real sign.

items.labeller_note: Only a few notes address hobby enthusiasm directly (one text about a spice rack); there is no guidance on duration, depth of engagement, or finishing projects that separates enthusiasm from novelty-seeking.
items.why: Follow-through, cost, repeated abandonment, and whether new interests displace obligations.

items.question: What would make me suspect hypomania rather than quick-to-act and novelty-seeking traits in a short text?
items.labeller_note: No note discusses hypomania or its markers (elevated or expansive mood, reduced need for sleep, increased energy, episodic change from baseline); the notes only separate impulsivity or irritability from ADHD and attribute them to stress, low mood or sleep loss.
items.why: Episodic change from baseline, reduced need for sleep, elevated mood, grandiosity, and duration versus lifelong pattern.

items.question: Which passages would colleagues read as ADHD-related, and what else could explain them?

key_points.text: Setting off to fetch one thing and returning with something else, with the original goal lost, is a specific lapse of working memory or goal-holding that raises the case for ADHD-related traits.
Such errand lapses are also explained by anxiety, caffeine, exam or job stress, tiredness, poor sleep, hunger or low mood, and are weak evidence on their own.
key_points.condition: especially with poor sleep or a new, high-pressure situation; single or short episodes

key_points.text: Repetition of the same intent-distraction-failure pattern in more than one instance, or a stated habit, makes it more telling than a single slip.
key_points.condition: if it recurs rather than being a one-off

key_points.text: Saying a job will take ten minutes and then overrunning is read by some as time misjudgment typical of ADHD.
A time-estimate overrun is often ordinary under high load, stress or poor sleep, especially when the text gives a reason or the writer notices it, and it is not by itself a time-management deficit.
key_points.condition: if an external cause or a competing task explains it, or the writer self-monitors

key_points.text: Preserved organisation, planning, self-monitoring, coping strategies and finishing of the main tasks argue against a pervasive ADHD picture and should not be overlooked.
key_points.condition: if competence holds across different tasks

key_points.text: Junior clinicians risk jumping to ADHD from one or two vivid incidents without weighing exam, job or sleep context; conversely, dismissing a repeated specific slip because the person is organised can miss it.
More information needed: whether the lapses are one-off or long-standing, occur in low-stress settings or with other tasks, and what sleep and baseline are like.

items.labeller_note: No note covers a new-job context or compensating with printed layouts directly beyond general organisation points; thresholds for how often is too often are missing.

signs.quote: The pallet of bulbs was meant to be ten minutes and I was still on it at lunch
came back with a trowel for a customer and no labels at all

other_explanations.quote: Slept badly again, the new flat has a boiler that clanks at night
other_explanations.explanation: Poor sleep from a noisy new flat could explain slips and slower work.

items.patient_text: Day nine at the garden centre. Mostly good. I learned the till on day two and have not had a single mismatch, and I was in before the manager both Mondays. The thing I keep doing is saying a job will take ten minutes. The pallet of bulbs was meant to be ten minutes and I was still on it at lunch. Then I went to fetch labels from the office and came back with a trowel for a customer and no labels at all. Lola had to remind me what I was after. Slept badly again, the new flat has a boiler that clanks at night, and I'm drinking more tea than I should. Tomorrow I'm doing the seed display, with the layout printed out and taped to the shelf, and the shift rota is already photographed on my phone.

items.question: Which passages would colleagues read as ADHD-related, and what else could explain them?

key_points.text: Sitting down to a hard task and drifting into unrelated reading (old messages, bus tickets) can be read as distractibility, though only mildly and not diagnostically.
key_points.condition: only if the drift occurs for non-emotional tasks too

key_points.text: Drifting away from an emotionally charged task is better explained by avoidance, grief, low mood, anxiety or poor sleep, a normal coping move when overwhelmed, rather than ADHD.
key_points.condition: when the task is tied to a bereavement or family illness

key_points.text: A distinguishing question is whether the stall is confined to the emotionally loaded task while easier tasks get done, and whether the writer would stall on it on a good day.
key_points.condition: a stall limited to the emotional task points away from a general initiation problem

key_points.text: Knowing exactly what to do yet not starting fits both an initiation problem and anxious avoidance, and is worth one question.
key_points.condition: depends on whether anxiety about getting it wrong is present

key_points.text: Underestimating the time a task needs is only weakly toward ADHD; it is often a calibration error under stress or workload change, and the writer did plan.
key_points.condition: if stress, sleep or workload change accounts for it

key_points.text: Some read a planned time that then slips as a hint of poor time estimation or delayed initiation.
key_points.condition: only as one episode

key_points.text: Deferring a dull task with words like soon or Sunday may be an ADHD sign, but a busy period and tiredness explain it equally.
key_points.condition: if the backlog began only when work got busier

key_points.text: Evidence of planning and follow-through (suit, train booked, reminders, concrete schedules, tasks done on time) points away from executive dysfunction.
key_points.condition: if such organisation is typical rather than a rare good day

key_points.text: A stated external cause (a family crisis, a lost boot) explains the delay in the text itself, so it should not be read as a trait.
More information needed: whether this stall is new or lifelong, whether the writer stalls on other tasks, and how mood and sleep have been.

items.labeller_note: No note speaks to the speech-writing task itself or to seeking blunt feedback; the notes give principles about avoidance versus distractibility and planning, not thresholds.

signs.quote: ended up reading old group chats instead, an hour gone before I'd typed a line
I thought I'd need a weekend for it

other_explanations.quote: Dad had his operation on Monday and I've been at the hospital most evenings
other_explanations.explanation: Worry and time spent at the hospital for a parent's illness could explain the delay.

items.patient_text: Hi Ruth, the speech for Tom's wedding. I have the opening and the ending done and they are good, I read them to Beth on the phone and she laughed in the right places. The middle is the trouble. Every evening this week I sat down to write it and ended up reading old group chats instead, an hour gone before I'd typed a line. I thought I'd need a weekend for it, and now the wedding is eleven days away. Dad had his operation on Monday and I've been at the hospital most evenings, so I'm not sure how much of it is that. The suit is back from the tailor, the train is booked, and I put the rings reminder in my calendar with two alerts. Can I send you a draft on Sunday and could you be blunt?

items.question: Which passages would colleagues read as ADHD-related, and what else could explain them?

key_points.text: Starting a task, being pulled into side tasks or tangents and leaving the original half done is the classic pattern read as ADHD-related, whether described as abandonment-restart or lost time.
The drift into a low-effort alternative that feels productive when the main task is dull (comparing apps, reorganising the desktop) is read as a procrastination loop that mildly raises the case.
key_points.condition: more telling if it occurs under no time pressure

key_points.text: Such side-task drifting also fits ordinary procrastination, boredom, low mood or grief, and says little about a lifelong pattern.
key_points.condition: if there is a stressor or low mood present

key_points.text: Heavy sleep loss (night shifts, an infant, noise) is a major confounder that explains lost time, forgetting why one entered a room and restarting tasks.
key_points.condition: if the lapses disappear when sleep is normal

key_points.text: Compensatory systems and advance planning (written lists, string line marked beforehand, timers, an app, a list used) show intact executive function and argue against ADHD.
key_points.condition: if such planning is typical for the writer

key_points.text: A single unfinished item noted as still to do is a list entry, not a pattern of unfinished business.
key_points.condition: if it is one item rather than repeated

key_points.text: Repeated intending without doing (invoices put off, plans made and not carried out) is a sign worth noting, though tiredness and a busy period can explain it.
key_points.condition: if it recurs and is not just a busy spell

key_points.text: A new stimulus triggering a new project (a video leading to a spice rack) can be impulsive redirection or ordinary enthusiasm or boredom.
key_points.condition: if it is repeated rather than a one-off

key_points.text: Junior clinicians may over-read fragmented task completion as ADHD while overlooking sleep disruption, and some may over-dismiss it as just tiredness and miss the lost intention despite a list.
More information needed: a sample from a rested or day-shift period, objective measures across settings, and whether the pattern is lifelong.

items.labeller_note: No note addresses reading about a tangent such as pricing unaffordable items, or an expensive digression as impulsivity.

signs.quote: spent a whole evening pricing up gravel bikes I can't afford
The cassette is still sitting on the shelf, half fitted

other_explanations.quote: the baby next door screams from two until four
other_explanations.explanation: Broken sleep from a noisy neighbour could explain a muddled head and unfinished jobs.

items.patient_text: Picked up a second-hand road bike for the commute and decided to replace the cassette myself. Watched two videos, bought the right tool, and the old one was off in twenty minutes, which felt great. Then I noticed the chain was worn so I started reading about chain wear, then about gearing, then spent a whole evening pricing up gravel bikes I can't afford. The cassette is still sitting on the shelf, half fitted. I'm also running on very little sleep, the baby next door screams from two until four, so my head is mush. Everything else is fine, I serviced the brakes last weekend with a list taped to the frame and it all went to plan. Does anyone know whether a worn chain ruins a new cassette?

items.question: Which passages would colleagues read as ADHD-related, and what else could explain them?

key_points.text: Cutting in or acting before the other person has answered is read as impulsive action, a classic ADHD trait.
key_points.condition: only if it recurs

key_points.text: Irritability or a sharp outburst in a rough patch, with grief, a break-up, low mood, strain or a short night, is better explained by stress than by a trait, especially if it is a single incident the writer owns.
key_points.condition: if one incident tied to a recent loss or strain

key_points.text: Acting before checking (ordering then measuring, a purchase on impulse) is read as an impulsive sequence or an executive slip.
key_points.condition: if part of a pattern of regretted actions

key_points.text: Such impulsive acts also fit a strong external reward (discount), low mood, a good deal, or an ordinary slip, and one incident is not diagnostic.
key_points.condition: if isolated rather than repeated

key_points.text: Evidence of planning, structure, strategies and completed work (plans, timers, train pass, food list, work delivered) argues against significant executive dysfunction.
key_points.condition: if the organisation is typical

key_points.text: Self-awareness and ownership of the mistake is a protective sign and suggests a slip rather than a constant state.
Delay or forgetfulness in the first weeks of a new job is largely explained by novelty, pressure and anxiety rather than ADHD.
key_points.condition: if these lapses are limited to the new setting

key_points.text: More information needed: whether the outburst or impulsive act is a one-off or a pattern across settings.

items.labeller_note: No note covers shaking after an outburst, emotional lability (tearing at adverts) since a bereavement, or sending a message without reading it back.

signs.quote: I cut in and told him exactly what I thought before my supervisor could signal me
I shook for ten minutes afterwards

other_explanations.quote: I've been like that since my gran's funeral last month, everything lands harder
other_explanations.explanation: Recent bereavement could explain heightened emotional reactions.

items.patient_text: Thursday. Second week at the call centre. Mostly I like it, the team are decent and I hit my target on Tuesday. But today a caller was rude about the refund rules and I cut in and told him exactly what I thought before my supervisor could signal me. She sent me for a break straight after. I shook for ten minutes afterwards. I've been like that since my gran's funeral last month, everything lands harder, I tear up at adverts. Then I sent a reply to the team chat without reading it back and had to apologise to Nadia for a typo that changed the meaning. Lunch was planned and sorted, I batch cooked on Sunday, and my notes for tomorrow's training are colour coded.

items.question: Which passages would colleagues read as ADHD-related, and what else could explain them?

key_points.text: A big gap between the planned time and the real time (a quick ten minute job taking weeks) is read as time underestimation or time blindness that mildly raises the case.
Time overruns are very often explained by stress, deadline pressure, poor sleep, anxiety or perfectionism, or ordinary underestimation of a task, and are weak evidence alone.
key_points.condition: if there is a clear stressor or one-off; check whether it recurs across settings

key_points.text: Doing other things first before opening the main task can be mild avoidance toward ADHD.
The same chores-first behaviour is often a conscious prioritisation, ordinary procrastination or an anxiety or stress response, not a trait.
key_points.condition: if a reason is stated and it is not the usual way of handling big tasks

key_points.text: A long deferral of an admin task with soon-type wording, or starting and stopping at the first friction point, is read as task-initiation difficulty.
The same delay fits burnout, fatigue or a busy period, or a recent change in work, and needs checking against the timeline.
key_points.condition: if the backlog arose only with a busier or changed workload

key_points.text: Self-monitoring, awareness of the slip, concrete time estimates based on data, and other tasks done well argue against significant executive dysfunction.
key_points.condition: if competence is typical

key_points.text: A task remembered late but completed in time reads as neutral or as a compensated lapse.
Junior clinicians may over-read a single time slip as ADHD while ignoring sleep, stress and context; others may under-read a specific initiation gap by calling it just busy.
More information needed: whether this is typical or an outlier, whether it also happens with emails or other tasks, and a sample from a low-stress period.

items.labeller_note: No note speaks to a three-week delay caused by a parent's repeated hospital admissions or to checking figures twice as a possible anxiety sign.

signs.quote: every time I opened the form I found something else to do first
I told myself it would be a quick ten minute job

other_explanations.quote: My mother is in and out of hospital and I'm driving up to see her most weekends
other_explanations.explanation: Caring for an ill parent leaves little time and attention for paperwork.

items.patient_text: Hello Karen, apologies for the late expenses claim for the Leeds trip. I meant to do it on the train home. I told myself it would be a quick ten minute job, then every time I opened the form I found something else to do first, the hotel invoice, the taxi receipts in my coat. It has been three weeks. My mother is in and out of hospital and I'm driving up to see her most weekends, so I've not been home much. The mileage figures are attached and I checked them twice. I also remembered to book next month's client dinner and to get the allergy details from all six of them, which I'm pleased about. Could you tell me the cut-off for this quarter?

items.question: Which passages would colleagues read as ADHD-related, and what else could explain them?

key_points.text: A digression the writer flags themselves ('nothing to do with anything', 'sorry', 'anyway') and then drops, returning to the point, shows intact self-monitoring and argues against disorganised thinking.
A sudden unrelated anecdote followed by a quick apology reads as the main sign of attentional drift or a poor filter, though only mildly.
key_points.condition: only if the tangent is habitual rather than a one-off

key_points.text: A tangent in a written message is as likely a chatty or associative style, nerves, a wish to relate, or a talkative person with a captive audience as a symptom.
Less experienced clinicians over-read a bounded digression or a long, apologetic message as disorganisation, hyperactivity or a poor filter.
The tangent is specific and bounded, and the rest of the text is structured and on task, so it does not amount to a ramble.
Ask whether such tangents are a habitual, constant feature of the writer's communication or occurred just this once.

items.labeller_note: Notes cover digressions and self-correction well but none address living alone and little social contact as an explanation for long, rambling text.

signs.quote: which reminds me, I have a brother in law who did roofing in Spain
I used to have a van, a Transit, and that's how I carried the felt the first time

other_explanations.quote: I live alone and don't talk to anyone most days, so forgive the waffle
other_explanations.explanation: Isolation can make someone chatty when given a chance to write.

items.patient_text: Question about my shed roof, sorry it's long. The felt started lifting at the corner in March, which reminds me, I have a brother in law who did roofing in Spain and he said something about battens but I forget what. Anyway my neighbour's shed has the same felt, his is fine, he put his on in the dry. I used to have a van, a Transit, and that's how I carried the felt the first time, but it went in December. Right. Question is simply: can I patch the corner or do I need to strip the whole thing? I've measured, it's 2.4 by 1.8 metres, and I have the roll, the clout nails and a ladder borrowed from Pete. I live alone and don't talk to anyone most days, so forgive the waffle.

items.question: Which passages would colleagues read as ADHD-related, and what else could explain them?

key_points.text: Setting off with one task, getting absorbed in another and losing the original (bins/toastie, glove boxes, fluid balance) is the classic goal-switching distraction pattern read toward ADHD.
Whether the derailment is a one-off or repeated across settings and long-standing decides how much weight it carries; one or two instances count for little.
key_points.condition: only if repeated across other tasks and settings

key_points.text: Sleep deprivation (a few hours a night) is a major confounder that can explain lost intentions and dropped tasks.
Situational stress, anxiety, caffeine, hunger, low motivation or a busy environment can equally explain the lapses.
Less experienced clinicians over-read a single task-switch lapse as ADHD without considering fatigue and context.
Planning ahead and proactive organising (alarm, prepared bag, written aids, asking IT early) shows intact planning and points away from a global executive deficit.
Losing the task while holding the physical reminder (list, sheet) is a more specific marker than ordinary forgetting.
key_points.condition: only if the person is well rested

key_points.text: Open, self-aware acknowledgement of the lapse and recovering from it indicates preserved monitoring.

signs.quote: started helping unpack someone else's crates, and the sheet was still in my hand an hour later

other_explanations.quote: I've had a rotten cold all week and slept maybe five hours a night
other_explanations.explanation: Illness and short sleep could explain feeling fuzzy and slipping on the task.

items.patient_text: Sunday. First month volunteering at the food bank. Sorted the tins by date on my own on Wednesday and Gill said it was the tidiest the shelves had been. I'm proud of that. Less proud of Saturday, when I was meant to be taking the delivery sheet to the van and got into a long conversation with a man about his dog, then started helping unpack someone else's crates, and the sheet was still in my hand an hour later when the driver left. I've had a rotten cold all week and slept maybe five hours a night, so I'm fuzzy. Monday I'm in at nine. I've put an alarm on my phone for eight, set out my bag, and written the bus times on a card in my wallet.

items.question: Which passages would colleagues read as ADHD-related, and what else could explain them?

key_points.text: Drifting to an unrelated low-effort side task when work is dull or aversive (reorganising desktop, comparing apps) is read mildly toward ADHD-style avoidance.
The same drift is equally ordinary procrastination, anxiety, perfectionism or low mood and grief, so it says little about a lifelong pattern.
key_points.condition: especially if mood is low or there is bereavement or stress

key_points.text: Abandoning a task halfway and having to restart or come back later is the classic task-abandonment pattern read toward ADHD.
Abandon-and-restart is common when fatigued, stressed or perfectionistic, and recognising and compensating (starting again from the top) is more like executive function under strain.
Ask whether the avoidance or abandonment is the writer's usual way of working or only situational or new.
Knowing and using a fix (timer, structure, external aid) shows the writer can regulate when helped.
key_points.condition: a learned compensation can occur in ADHD as well as in anyone with a work style

key_points.text: Good organisation elsewhere (early every day, structured routine, strong organising and verification behaviours) counters a pervasive executive deficit.
key_points.condition: new, high-structure settings may flatter performance

key_points.text: Less experienced clinicians over-read avoidance as ADHD while ignoring context such as grief, low mood or fatigue.

items.labeller_note: No note speaks to the writer's specific stall at one aversive form-filling step or to visual or reading difficulty as a cause.

signs.quote: the questions about the value of each room defeated me and I drifted off to the garden
I've picked it up four times since and always stopped at the same page

other_explanations.quote: my eyes tire quickly now, and I changed my glasses last month
other_explanations.explanation: New glasses and tired eyes could make long small-print forms hard to finish.

items.patient_text: Dear Mr Hale, thank you for your patience about the contents insurance form. I started it the day you sent it and got through the first three pages, then the questions about the value of each room defeated me and I drifted off to the garden. I've picked it up four times since and always stopped at the same page. I'm 58 and my eyes tire quickly now, and I changed my glasses last month so reading small print is still a nuisance. The rest of my paperwork is up to date, the car tax and the boiler service are both booked, and I keep a folder for every year. I can finish it by Friday if I do a page a day. Would that be all right?

items.question: Which passages would colleagues read as ADHD-related, and what else could explain them?

key_points.text: Underestimating how long a task will take (planned one hour, took three) is the classic time-estimation marker read toward ADHD.
key_points.condition: only if it recurs across settings rather than once

key_points.text: The overrun is equally explained by fatigue, poor sleep, workload, task difficulty or stress, and a single instance is noise.
Having made a plan and noticing and owning the slip suggests a calibration error with intact monitoring, not a failure to plan or initiate.
Buying something large on a short window and checking fit or suitability afterwards (measuring after ordering) is read as an impulsive, act-before-check sequence.
The impulsive purchase could equally reflect a good deal or payday impulse, low mood, exhaustion or a shopping habit.
key_points.condition: depending on whether it is an isolated incident or a pattern

key_points.text: Organised, completed preparation and booked-ahead plans elsewhere point away from a pervasive executive deficit.
Planning ahead for a week is strong evidence against executive dysfunction.
It matters whether the planned, organised behaviour is typical or a one-off burst of effort.
key_points.condition: consistency across tasks and over time

key_points.text: Less experienced clinicians over-read a time overrun or backlog as ADHD and overlook situational factors such as workload or tiredness.

items.labeller_note: No note addresses skipping preparation (not taping) to press on, or optimistic deferral as such.

signs.quote: I said it would be a morning job and it is now six in the evening with two walls done
I bought the paint on the way home from work after seeing a colour card in the shop

other_explanations.quote: I'm tired because of the new shift pattern at the warehouse, early starts all week
other_explanations.explanation: Early starts and tiredness could explain the slow pace.

items.patient_text: Saturday. Painting the spare room. I said it would be a morning job and it is now six in the evening with two walls done. I didn't tape the skirting because I wanted to crack on, and I bought the paint on the way home from work after seeing a colour card in the shop, only checking afterwards that it would suit the room. It does, luckily. The ceiling was already done last weekend, with dust sheets down and everything covered, and I cleaned every brush straight after. I'm tired because of the new shift pattern at the warehouse, early starts all week, so I might be doing it slower than I think. Dave rang and I told him I'd finish tomorrow, we'll see.

items.question: Which passages would colleagues read as ADHD-related, and what else could explain them?

key_points.text: Walking into a room and forgetting why is a very common slip that deserves little weight, especially when it has happened only twice.
Losing the purpose of a task is a mild working-memory marker that could point toward ADHD if it forms a pattern with other lapses.
key_points.condition: only if part of a wider pattern of lapses

key_points.text: Severe sleep deprivation is a major confounder and explains forgetting and fuzziness on its own.
The first weeks of a new job, with novelty, effort and anxiety, make executive slips more common and are the most parsimonious explanation.
Less experienced clinicians over-read such lapses as ADHD and miss the new-job and sleep context.
Organised, reliable performance elsewhere (early every day, systematic logging, on-time delivery, pre-packed preparation) argues against a pervasive deficit.
Writing notes or on the hand as a memory aid can be a compensation for shaky recall or just a tired person's workaround.
To judge whether the muddle will ease, ask whether it is new since the job or lifelong, whether it is frequent, and how it looks in calm, well-rested samples.

items.labeller_note: No note speaks to the writer's specific difficulty holding spoken orders in mind or whether such difficulty eases with adaptation.

signs.quote: A customer reads out six items and by the time I reach the counter I've lost two of them
walked to the cold room for butter and stood there looking at the shelves with no idea why

other_explanations.quote: Obviously I'm on three or four hours of sleep
other_explanations.explanation: Very short sleep from early starts could explain the muddle.

items.patient_text: Three weeks as a baker's assistant and I love it. I get up at three, the bread has never been late, and Mario trusted me with the sourdough on my own last Thursday. What worries me is the orders. A customer reads out six items and by the time I reach the counter I've lost two of them, so I've started jotting on a scrap of paper, which slows things down. Yesterday I walked to the cold room for butter and stood there looking at the shelves with no idea why. Obviously I'm on three or four hours of sleep, and my girlfriend says anyone would be vague on that. Does the muddle ease once the early starts become normal? The closing checklist I do properly every night, and the till has balanced on every shift.

items.question: Which passages would colleagues read as ADHD-related, and what else could explain them?

key_points.text: Snapping at someone in public and acting before they could answer reads as irritability and impulsivity, mildly toward ADHD-related emotional dysregulation.
key_points.condition: only if more than a single incident

key_points.text: Such an outburst has a better explanation in stress, strain, low mood, a short night or a bad stretch than in a trait.
The writer owns the outburst and is otherwise calm and in control, and the rest of the day was fine, which argues against a regulation trait.
Generalised low mood, whether chronic or situational, explains reduced drive and irritability and must be separated from ADHD.
key_points.condition: depends on whether the low mood is persistent or new

key_points.text: Strong functioning elsewhere (finishing induction fast, early every day, a good first week, structured tasks, planning) counters a pervasive executive deficit.
key_points.condition: a new, structured setting may flatter performance

key_points.text: A written reminder or other practical aid is a compensatory strategy, equally practical or a sign of good insight.
The writer's own explanation, that newness or context accounts for the difficulty, is taken seriously as plausible.
Ask whether the pattern is new or occurs across other contexts and workplaces.
Less experienced clinicians over-read an emotional outburst as ADHD without weighing the context.

items.labeller_note: No note addresses pregnancy or hormonal changes as an explanation, or tearfulness over a small trigger.

signs.quote: I nearly cried, then I was sharp with him for the rest of the afternoon

other_explanations.quote: We found out three weeks ago that we're expecting, and I'm told everything feels bigger at the moment
other_explanations.explanation: Early pregnancy can heighten emotional responses.

items.patient_text: Tuesday. Worst bit of today: Kamil moved my desk plant to the window without asking and I nearly cried, then I was sharp with him for the rest of the afternoon. It's a plant. I went to the toilets and breathed until it passed. Everything else at the new office is going well. I finished the onboarding checklist in four days and my manager said nobody had done it that fast. We found out three weeks ago that we're expecting, and I'm told everything feels bigger at the moment, so that may be some of it. I apologised to Kamil at five and he laughed, thank goodness. I've put a reminder in my phone to buy a thank you card for the receptionist.

items.question: Which passages would colleagues read as ADHD-related, and what else could explain them?

key_points.text: Buying something large within a short window and checking the practicalities afterwards is read as an impulsive act-before-checking sequence, toward ADHD.
Such a purchase may equally reflect an external reward (discount, good deal), payday habit, low mood, exhaustion, or a reversibility strategy.
Ask whether the purchase is isolated or part of a pattern of regretted spending, and whether it needs an external reward.
Poor sleep is a strong physiological confounder of judgement and executive function.
Organised, planned behaviour elsewhere (planned ahead for a week, completed tasks, switched to a monthly pass, structured routine) argues against a global deficit.
Whether that organisation is typical or only a high-stakes or one-off burst needs checking.
Spending on or browsing a side purchase instead of the task (comparing and buying apps) is read mildly toward impulsivity.
key_points.condition: only if it is a habitual pattern

key_points.text: Writers who note their own slip ('obviously', 'caught myself') show self-monitoring and suggest a slip rather than a constant state.
Less experienced clinicians over-read the purchase or side-task behaviour as definite ADHD, missing context such as sleep, grief or low mood.

items.labeller_note: No note speaks to the campervan browsing as a separate sign or to purchasing a vehicle specifically.

signs.quote: by seven I'd paid the deposit
Didn't check the service history until I got home
I'm already looking at campervans online, and I've saved three listings

other_explanations.quote: It has been a week of loud music upstairs, so I got about four hours a night
other_explanations.explanation: Noise and poor sleep could cloud judgement and speed up decisions.

items.patient_text: Bought a car on Friday. Went to look at a cheap hatchback after work 'just to see', and by seven I'd paid the deposit. Didn't check the service history until I got home, and it's patchy, so I'll have to ring the garage on Monday. Also I'm already looking at campervans online, and I've saved three listings, not seriously. Mostly. To be fair I had a budget, I'd saved for it for a year, the insurance quote was already sorted and the MOT date is in my calendar. It has been a week of loud music upstairs, so I got about four hours a night, and my judgement may be a bit off. Anyone else buy a car this way?

items.question: Which passages would colleagues read as ADHD-related, and what else could explain them?

key_points.text: Stalling on one emotionally loaded task (the folder or the bedroom) while other tasks are done reads as grief-related avoidance rather than a cognitive initiation deficit, so it lowers the case for ADHD.
key_points.condition: when the stall is tied to an emotionally charged object or task and not seen across neutral tasks

key_points.text: Competent, well-organised performance on other demanding tasks (clearing the garage, finishing the practical admin, smooth execution once started) argues against general executive dysfunction.
Grief, poor sleep and bereavement stress can by themselves produce brain fog, memory slips and difficulty starting tasks, so they must be separated out before attributing difficulty to ADHD.
key_points.condition: while the bereavement is recent

key_points.text: Low mood or depressive inertia is the main alternative explanation for trouble starting tasks and for avoidance, and can mimic executive dysfunction; ask whether the low mood is persistent or situational.
key_points.condition: if mood has been low and the avoidance is driven by drive and emotion rather than distractibility

key_points.text: A stall before starting a task, with the writer unable to say why, can be read as task-initiation difficulty, but it is weak evidence when isolated.
key_points.condition: only if it recurs across settings, including neutral tasks and work

key_points.text: A single pause or stall is just as easily explained by fatigue, low mood, anxiety or ordinary reluctance to start an unpleasant chore, and the writer resolving it quickly argues against a trait.
key_points.condition: when the stall is a one-off and the task is eventually completed

key_points.text: Ask whether the stalling is a recurring pattern or a one-off; a current sample of work or decision-making separate from the grief would show whether difficulties exist in other contexts.
key_points.condition: needed before judging a trait

key_points.text: A junior clinician may over-read emotionally specific avoidance or a single stall as ADHD, missing the competence shown elsewhere and the confounders.

items.labeller_note: No note covers a grief-sorting text directly; the closest are bereavement-folder avoidance notes and counter-stall notes from other texts, and none give a way to tell grief from ADHD beyond context and recurrence.

signs.quote: I thought a weekend would do the kitchen and it did not
just moved the same box from the landing to the stairs and back

other_explanations.explanation: Recent bereavement could explain slowness and avoidance.

other_explanations.quote: it's very hard to be in there
other_explanations.explanation: Emotional pain of being in the house could explain avoiding the task.

items.patient_text: Sunday. Third weekend at Mum's house, sorting. We lost her in January. I thought a weekend would do the kitchen and it did not, I've only done two cupboards. Standing in the hall with the bin bags I could not start on the bedroom, just moved the same box from the landing to the stairs and back. My brother thinks I'm avoiding it, and I probably am, it's very hard to be in there. What I did do well: rang the solicitor, sent the certificates to the bank, and cancelled the paper delivery and the gas account in one afternoon. Home by six, soup, early night.

items.question: Which passages would colleagues read as ADHD-related, and what else could explain them?

key_points.text: Attention slipping in a long sustained task, with lost stretches of time or drifting to another activity, is the kind of sign colleagues read as possibly ADHD-related inattention or distractibility.
key_points.condition: stronger if it recurs across settings and when not tired

key_points.text: Lost time and drift are very often explained by fatigue after long shifts, sleep loss, exam or deadline stress, anxiety or caffeine, so a tired writer coming from a ten-hour shift would fade for anyone.
key_points.condition: if the episodes occur when tired or stressed and not when rested

key_points.text: Drifting off into tidying or low-value activity when the material is dull or goes on too long can be ordinary procrastination or boredom, and it is bounded when the writer has a fix for it.
key_points.condition: depends on whether it occurs only with dull or over-long tasks

key_points.text: Making a plan, using external scaffolds (timetable, alarms, phone away, timed blocks) and meeting deadlines or completing homework on time point away from pervasive executive dysfunction and show active self-management.

Planning and compensatory strategies do not exclude ADHD: they can coexist with it, and deadline success may depend on external structure or a waiting person, so they should be weighed rather than treated as proof against.
key_points.condition: success tied to external deadlines or good setting

key_points.text: It is unclear whether the coping strategies are long-standing or newly invented, and whether they work consistently across tasks; this should be asked.
key_points.condition: needed to interpret the strategy evidence

key_points.text: Ask whether the drifting is typical across work and social settings and in other contexts, or an outlier tied to current stress and short sleep.
Less experienced clinicians tend to over-read lost minutes and coffee intake as ADHD while missing the structure, insight and deadlines the writer shows.

items.labeller_note: No note speaks to lecture-specific attention fading after about twenty minutes or to drawing boxes; the notes cover distraction, fatigue and compensation in other texts.

signs.quote: then she's on to depreciation schedules and my mind slides off
I catch myself drawing boxes on my notes

other_explanations.quote: I'm also coming straight from a ten hour shift in the kitchen
other_explanations.explanation: Tiredness after a long working day could explain fading in class.

items.patient_text: Evening bookkeeping class, week five. I like the teacher and I've done every homework on the day it was set, even the ledger one. The lectures are the problem. The first twenty minutes I'm with her, then she's on to depreciation schedules and my mind slides off, and I catch myself drawing boxes on my notes. I missed the whole last section on Tuesday. I'm also coming straight from a ten hour shift in the kitchen, with my feet aching and a sandwich in my bag, so I'd probably fade for anyone. I taped my timetable inside the front of my folder and set phone alarms for the break.

items.question: Which passages would colleagues read as ADHD-related, and what else could explain them?

key_points.text: A task that drifts into an unrelated activity (going for one thing and returning with something else, the original left untouched) is read as a possible sign of distractibility or a working-memory slip.
key_points.condition: stronger if the pattern is repeated and long-standing

key_points.text: Such drifts are commonly explained by anxiety, caffeine, deadline pressure, fatigue or poor sleep, and one bounded episode should not be taken as the whole diagnosis.
key_points.condition: if stressors are present or the pattern is not chronic and pervasive

key_points.text: Sleep deprivation from an external cause (a child's illness, noise) explains lapses and irritability and not a stable trait; check whether the difficulties are present when rested.
key_points.condition: while the sleep disruption lasts

key_points.text: Underestimating how long a task will take is ordinary when the text gives specific external reasons, and it is not evidence of time blindness by itself.
key_points.condition: when concrete reasons for the overrun are stated

key_points.text: Careful advance planning (fixed arrangements, lists, workable plan B) points away from ADHD-type disorganisation.
A repeated gap between intending and doing is worth weight even when tiredness is an easy explanation, so the deferral wording should not be dismissed.
key_points.condition: stronger if the intention-action gap is long-standing

key_points.text: Baseline information is missing: whether the lapses occurred before the current stressor or busy period, and when rested.
key_points.condition: needed before attributing the pattern

key_points.text: Junior clinicians may over-read one or two episodes as ADHD when anxiety, caffeine and short sleep explain much of them.

items.labeller_note: Nothing speaks to the oven timer episode or to hosting and cooking timing specifically; notes cover distraction drifts and sleep-loss confounds from other texts.

signs.quote: I reckon I need ninety minutes for the veg

items.patient_text: Hi Ana, thanks for offering to come early on Saturday. The menu is fixed, lamb, roast veg, and the lemon tart you like, and I shopped on Wednesday with a list so there are no gaps. Where I'm worried is the timing. I reckon I need ninety minutes for the veg, and last time it was much longer because I started chopping, put the radio on and found myself alphabetising the spice rack. The oven timer also went off twice before I remembered what it was for. I've been up with my son's earache all week so I'm not at my sharpest. Could you bring a few chairs? I've counted and we are two short.
